verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), chapter 8 TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS, Very Short Answer question 30, book p.88. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1 split rewards clearing the sec α out of the bracket first and the matching factorisation of the two sides second. Paper position: Maths-1A Section A runs Q1 to Q10 at 2 marks each, all compulsory, under the 2026-27 pattern; Trigonometric Ratios and Transformations holds two of those ten slots. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Checked numerically at α = 37°, 100° and 215°: the two sides agree to ten decimal places (0.8688246899, 0.0593981342 and 0.8917656271). Note on the condition: the reduced identity cos⁴α + 2cos²α sin²α = 1 − sin⁴α holds for every α, but the printed left side contains sec α, so the statement as printed needs cos α ≠ 0. That condition is written on the page in the student's own lines, not left here.

recall_prompt: Say what you would do with the sec α bracket, and say what both sides reduce to.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Replace 1/sec²α by cos²α
steps.margin_note: First mark. sec α is written on the left, so cos α ≠ 0 is part of the statement. The bracket is only sin²α in disguise.
steps.memory_tip: 1/sec²α is cos²α, so the bracket 1 − 1/sec²α is just sin²α.
lines: sec α is written, so cos α ≠ 0.

recall.must_convey: That 1/sec²α is cos²α, so the bracket becomes sin²α and the left side is cos⁴α + 2cos²α sin²α.
accept: one over sec squared alpha is cos squared alpha so the bracket is one minus cos squared which is sin squared
the bracket is just sin squared alpha
replace one by sec squared with cos squared and the left side becomes cos to the fourth plus two cos squared sin squared
one by sec square ante cos square, so bracket sin square avutundi
clear the sec alpha out first
reject: one minus sin to the fourth

steps.why: The bracket is written with sec α only to hide sin²α. Replacing 1/sec²α by cos²α turns it into 1 − cos²α, which is sin²α, and the left side becomes a plain expression in sin α and cos α. Writing sec α at all is what makes cos α ≠ 0 part of the statement.
common_mistakes: Using sec α without noting that cos α must not be 0.

steps.label: Factor both sides
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Take cos²α out on the left and use the difference of two squares on the right. Both sides land on cos²α(1 + sin²α).
steps.memory_tip: Both sides collapse to cos²α(1 + sin²α). On the right use 1 − sin⁴α = (1 − sin²α)(1 + sin²α).

recall.must_convey: That both sides reduce to cos²α(1 + sin²α), the right side by factoring 1 − sin⁴α as (1 − sin²α)(1 + sin²α).
accept: take cos squared out on the left and it becomes cos squared into one plus sin squared
one minus sin to the fourth is one minus sin squared into one plus sin squared which is cos squared into one plus sin squared
both sides come to cos squared alpha into one plus sin squared alpha
rendu sides cos square into one plus sin square vastundi
factor the right side as a difference of two squares
reject: one over sec squared is cos squared

steps.why: Both sides reduce to the same thing, cos²α(1 + sin²α). On the left the factor cos²α comes out and cos²α + sin²α becomes 1; on the right 1 − sin⁴α is a difference of two squares whose first factor is cos²α.
common_mistakes: Stopping at cos⁴α + 2cos²α sin²α without factoring.
